# Speak to your Parser: Interactive Text-to-SQL with Natural Language Feedback

[All reading notes](../reading-notes.md) · [Catalog entry](../README.md#splash)

**Full paper read · 2026-11-09**

[Original source](https://aclanthology.org/2020.acl-main.187.pdf) · ACL 2020 proceedings, pages 2065-2077

**Reading coverage:** All thirteen PDF pages, Sections 1-7 and Appendix A.1-A.3 including annotator instructions, interface description and explanation templates; tables and figure captions read.

## Research question

Users may identify errors in an initial query through plain-language explanations without being able to edit SQL directly.

## Method

Seq2Struct errors on Spider receive template-based explanations and short crowdsourced correction feedback, including paraphrases. Models consume the original question, schema, wrong parse and supplied feedback to predict a corrected parse.

## Evaluation

SPLASH has 9,314 question-feedback pairs with database-separated splits. Correction is scored using Spider exact set match. End-to-end accuracy is estimated from initial parser accuracy plus correction success on explanation-supported failures; a small additional set tests EditSQL errors.

## What the results support

EditSQL with feedback reaches 25.16% correction accuracy, while shuffled feedback reduces it to 5.6%. Corrections transfer less effectively to errors from a stronger parser. The headline 81.5% human estimate is the proportion of 200 sampled feedback items judged complete.

## Limits and qualifications

The human estimate is not a measured human SQL-correction experiment. Explanation-template coverage limits eligible failures; feedback is recorded, capped in length, and sometimes partial. The task explicitly assumes fully specified questions rather than asking agents to detect ambiguity.

## Relevance to reliable Text-to-SQL

A useful controlled test of incorporating feedback, with a different objective from choosing clarification questions or refusing unsupported requests.
